newsitem.title: USA: Clinton briefed on Albright family history.
newsitem.headline: Clinton briefed on Albright family history.

text.p: The White House said on Tuesday President Bill Clinton was briefed on the discovery that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright appears to be of Jewish ancestry and said this in no way complicated her ability to encourage peace in the Middle East.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters Albright herself briefed the president and Vice President Al Gore on the matter on Monday.
"The president said it was a fascinating story and encouraged Madeleine to find our more, to look into her family history," McCurry said. "He thought it was fascinating."

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Monday that, based on newly available information, the Czech-born Albright believed it was "more than likely" her grandparents were Jewish and three of them died in the Holocaust.

The Washington Post recently researched Albright's background and reported on Tuesday that more than a dozen of her relatives, including three grandparents, were killed as Jewish victims of the Holocaust in Czechoslovakia.

"Based on the information she has received, Secretary Albright believes it is more than likely that these events occurred," Burns said. But he said Albright, 59, and her family felt a need to follow up on the Post's research and confirm their genealogy themselves.

Burns said Albright had believed from an early age that she was Roman Catholic and only now was coming to understand her heritage was Jewish. She was raised as a Catholic but later became an Episcopalian.
Asked on Tuesday if the discovery might in any way complicate Albright's efforts to encourage the Middle East peace process, McCurry replied: "No."

"There are three great monotheistic traditions that consider the Middle East a holy place and we have talented diplomats from all three religious traditions that work on the Middle East peace process," he added.
Albright was 2 years old when her parents left Czechoslovakia in 1939, less than two weeks after the Nazi occupation. The family eventually came to the United States.
